The border drawn between India and Pakistan in Punjab and Bengal in 1947, named for the British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe, who chaired the two boundary commissions. It was made public on 17 August, two days after independence.

Radcliffe had never been to India. He was given about five weeks and used old district maps and census counts of religion. Each commission had two judges named by Congress and two by the Muslim League, who disagreed, so the decisions fell to him. Hard questions were whether Lahore or Amritsar would go to Pakistan, what to do with the Gurdaspur district (which gave India access to Kashmir) and the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Radcliffe left the country soon after and was said to have burned his papers.

People did not know which side of the line they lived on until after the deadline. Some 10 to 15 million crossed it. Deaths were in the hundreds of thousands, with estimates up to two million.

The line was a cause of the Partition violence and still marks the India-Pakistan border.
